flashcards.q: What is BOLA and why has it remained #1 on OWASP's API Top 10 since 2019?
flashcards.a: Broken Object Level Authorization: an endpoint authenticates the caller correctly but never checks whether that specific caller owns the specific object ID requested. Remains #1 because it requires zero sophisticated technique (just increment an ID) and is trivially easy to introduce by forgetting one check on one endpoint. Present in ~40% of real API attacks.

flashcards.q: Can an API gateway close BOLA vulnerabilities?
flashcards.a: No -- a gateway can validate token validity and rate limits, but has no business-logic knowledge of which specific object a specific caller legitimately owns. Object-level authorization must be implemented in the service that has access to the ownership data.

flashcards.q: What is mass assignment and how is it fixed?
flashcards.a: An endpoint binds an entire client-supplied request body directly onto an internal model with no allowlist, letting a client set fields never meant to be client-writable (is_admin, role) simply by including them in the JSON. Fixed via a framework schema/serializer layer (Pydantic, DRF serializers, Rails strong_parameters) enforcing an explicit allowlist.

flashcards.q: What two 2019 OWASP API categories were merged into API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization, and why?
flashcards.a: Excessive Data Exposure (read side: server returns whole object, trusts client not to display sensitive fields) and Mass Assignment (write side: client body bound onto model unchecked) were merged because they share the same root cause: insufficient control over which object PROPERTIES a caller can read/write.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between BOLA (API1) and Broken Function Level Authorization (API5)?
flashcards.a: BOLA is about which OBJECT a caller can access (allowed to call the endpoint, shouldn't access this specific instance). API5 is about whether the caller can invoke the FUNCTION/endpoint at all, independent of any object -- e.g. an admin route reachable by any user because the restriction only existed in the UI, never server-side.

flashcards.q: What is the GraphQL-specific flavor of unrestricted resource consumption, and its fix?
flashcards.a: A single deeply-nested recursive query (user{posts{comments{author{posts{...}}}}}) causes combinatorial fan-out against the database while looking like one request to a rate limiter. Fix: query complexity/depth analysis assigning cost per field/relation, rejecting queries exceeding a configured maximum, in addition to standard rate limiting.

flashcards.q: Why is rate limiting alone insufficient for API6 (unrestricted access to sensitive business flows)?
flashcards.a: A sophisticated attacker distributes requests across many accounts and IPs specifically to stay under any single-source rate-limit threshold -- each individual request looks legitimate. Needs controls tied to a durable identity signal: verified-account caps, behavioral/device fingerprinting, CAPTCHA/proof-of-work at high-risk points.

flashcards.q: What is improper inventory management (API9) and why is it a process failure, not just technical?
flashcards.a: APIs accumulate stale endpoints/versions (a deprecated-in-docs v1 that was never actually decommissioned) that remain live, unmonitored, and unpatched. Fix requires an enforced decommission date with monitoring confirming zero remaining traffic before removal -- documentation alone doesn't stop traffic.

flashcards.q: In a multi-tenant SaaS API, why should tenant scoping be enforced at the database layer, not just application-layer WHERE clauses?
flashcards.a: Relying purely on application-layer discipline means one forgotten WHERE tenant_id=? clause anywhere in a large codebase is a full cross-tenant data leak -- the same 'one missed check across many endpoints' failure mode that makes BOLA the top vulnerability. DB-layer row-level security provides a structural backstop independent of every query author remembering the filter.

flashcards.q: Why is 'our API is only called by our official mobile app' not a valid reason to skip API security controls?
flashcards.a: A server has no reliable way to verify a request actually came from the official app vs a reverse-engineered client or replayed traffic -- any client-side identifier can be extracted or spoofed. Even app attestation (App Attest/Play Integrity) attests the CLIENT, not the specific request's authorization, so it's complementary, never a substitute for object/function-level checks.
